name: Capabilities and human development

thinkers.name: Amartya Sen
thinkers.note: Built the argument across three decades, starting from a question about what equality is even measuring. The 1998 Nobel citation named welfare economics, social choice and the study of famine, which are the same project approached three times.

thinkers.name: Mahbub ul Haq
thinkers.note: Pakistani economist who had spent the 1960s building growth plans and concluded they measured the wrong thing. He turned Sen's philosophy into an index and an annual report, over Sen's initial objection that a single number would flatten the idea.

thinkers.name: Martha Nussbaum
thinkers.note: Argued, against Sen, that the approach needs a specified list of central capabilities if it is to ground claims of justice rather than only evaluation.

claim: Development should be measured by what people are actually able to do and to be, because income and even goods say nothing about what a particular person can convert them into.
summary: Sen's opening move is a question about measurement: equality of what? Income treats a rupee as a rupee whoever holds it. Utility treats satisfaction as the currency, which means a person who has adapted to deprivation and stopped wanting much scores well. Goods themselves are no better, because the same bicycle gives mobility to one person and nothing to another.

The answer is to evaluate at the level of functionings, the things a person actually manages to do and be, and capabilities, the set of functionings genuinely open to them. What sits between a resource and a functioning is a conversion factor: a disability, a caste rule about who may draw water, a road that floods, a norm about where a woman may walk after dark. Two households with the same income can have entirely different capability sets, and the difference is not a matter of preference.

Haq's contribution was to make it operational and public. The first Human Development Report in 1990 opened by saying that people are the real wealth of a nation, and put a three-part index next to GDP: a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living. Sen was uneasy about compressing the idea into one number and joined anyway, on the argument that a crude index that competes with GNP is more use than a refined idea that does not.

With Jean Drèze, Sen then applied it to India across three books, and the argument that came out is about public action. India's record on the things the approach measures has lagged its record on income growth, and the gap is not explained by poverty alone, since poorer countries and poorer Indian states have done better on schooling, immunisation and child nutrition.

axis_notes.allocation: Public provision for health, education and social security, with markets left in place for most production. Sen has been consistently unwilling to treat the market itself as the enemy.
axis_notes.priority: Distribution is the measurement, not a later correction. Growth matters because of what it buys, and the approach exists to keep asking whether it bought anything.
axis_notes.hierarchy: Conversion factors are where caste, gender and disability enter, and they enter as causes of different outcomes from the same resources. Sen's work on missing women and on cooperative conflict inside households is the clearest case.
axis_notes.agency: Both, in a specific arrangement: public action means a state that provides and a public that argues, with democratic discussion doing the work of setting priorities.

layers.title: The question is what to measure
layers.text: Income, utility and the bundle of goods each fail in a way that can be shown with an example rather than argued about. Income ignores what a rupee buys for this person. Utility rewards adaptation to deprivation. Goods ignore what the person can do with them. Sen's 1979 lecture puts the three side by side and asks for a fourth.

layers.title: Conversion is where people differ
layers.text: Between a resource and what a person does with it sits a set of conversion factors: the body, the household, the neighbourhood, the law and the norms. A wheelchair user and an able-bodied person given the same transport budget do not get the same mobility. A woman in a household that decides for her does not get the same schooling from the same fees waived.

layers.title: So evaluate functionings and capabilities
layers.text: A functioning is something achieved: being nourished, being literate, appearing in public without shame. A capability is the set of functionings a person could actually choose. The distinction carries the freedom: fasting and starving are the same functioning and entirely different capability sets, and an evaluation that cannot tell them apart is measuring the wrong thing.

layers.title: Entitlement, and why famines happen
layers.text: Sen's earlier work is the same argument applied to food. A famine is a failure of what a person is entitled to command, not necessarily of what exists to be commanded. The Bengal famine of 1943 killed on a scale that food availability alone does not explain; wages, prices and who could exchange what for food do explain it. The lesson generalises: entitlements are the mechanism, and they can collapse while supply is intact.

layers.title: Measured, published, and compared
layers.text: Haq's index: life expectancy, education, and income at diminishing returns, combined into one number and published every year for every country. Its purpose is competitive rather than analytical. A government that can point to its growth rate and is shown its position on human development has to answer for the gap, and that answer happens in public.

layers.title: Which makes public action the instrument
layers.text: If the gap between income and capability is created by conversion factors, then the things that close it are schooling, health services, nutrition, water and social security, and the thing that makes governments provide them is public argument. Drèze and Sen's Indian work turns on this: a democracy with a free press has prevented famine and has not prevented endemic undernutrition, because one is dramatic and reported and the other is not.

evidence.claim: Income growth does not carry human development with it automatically.
evidence.finding: India is the standing example. Growth after 1991 was rapid and the improvement in child nutrition was not: the National Family Health Survey rounds recorded child stunting falling slowly from around 48 per cent in 2005-06 to roughly 38 per cent in 2015-16 and about 36 per cent in 2019-21, leaving India worse on this measure than countries with a fraction of its income per head. The pattern is old enough to have a name, the Asian enigma, given to it in 1996.
evidence.source: National Family Health Survey rounds 3, 4 and 5, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; Ramalingaswami, Jonsson and Rohde on the Asian enigma

evidence.claim: A famine can happen without a fall in food availability.
evidence.finding: The entitlement account of the 1943 Bengal famine has been argued over for forty years and has largely held, in the sense that nobody now explains the famine by supply alone. The sharpest challenges, including Bowbrick's, dispute Sen's specific availability figures rather than the general claim that exchange entitlements can collapse independently of supply, and the mechanism is now standard in famine early-warning practice.
evidence.source: Amartya Sen, Poverty and Famines; and the subsequent literature including Peter Bowbrick's critique

evidence.claim: A single index can move governments.
evidence.finding: It did, and in a way that is measurable in behaviour rather than outcomes. National and state human development reports became routine, India's states began publishing their own, and the reporting of an HDI rank is now a fixed feature of the political argument. Whether the reporting improved the underlying numbers is a separate question the index cannot answer about itself.
evidence.source: UNDP Human Development Report series from 1990; Indian state human development reports

evidence.claim: Public provision, not income, does most of the work.
evidence.finding: Supported by the within-India comparison that Drèze and Sen built the argument on. Kerala reached life expectancy and literacy levels far above what its income per head predicted, on a record of school provision, public health and land reform going back to the princely states and sustained by electoral competition. The comparison is genuinely informative and it is one case, which is the standing weakness of the argument.
evidence.source: Jean Drèze and Amartya Sen, India: Economic Development and Social Opportunity

unsettled: The approach is much better at evaluation than at prescription, and its own proponents say so. Knowing that a girl's schooling is blocked by a conversion factor does not say which instrument removes it, and the list of capabilities that matter is either left open, as Sen prefers, which makes it hard to use for policy, or specified, as Nussbaum does, which raises the question of whose list it is. What has not been resolved is the aggregation problem the Human Development Index papered over: the index weights three things equally because there is no principled way to weight them at all, and everyone involved knew that in 1990.
india: Two of the three people who built this were from the subcontinent and the Indian material is not an application but a source. The famine work is Bengal. The missing women calculation is South Asian demography. The public action argument was assembled from the difference between Kerala and Uttar Pradesh. It is also the theory with the deepest institutional presence here, through the state human development reports, the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act's rights framing, and the Right to Education, and that presence is itself worth noticing: an approach designed to resist a single number produced a single number, and the number is what travelled.
compare_note: Conversion factors and caste are the same observation from two directions: the same resource does different work depending on who holds it and where.
contrast_note: Rostow's endpoint is high mass consumption. This approach exists to say that consumption is a means whose value depends entirely on what a particular person can do with it.
